number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 409, 467, 468, 471 and 420 IPC; finally upheld: Not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the Power of Attorney (PoA) was valid and that the PoA-holder was authorized to execute sale deeds and receive consideration on behalf of the land-owners/principals.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the informant and others had not received any response from the PoA-holder to their legal notice, indicating a lack of cooperation and potential dispute between the land-owners/principals and the PoA-holder.
bail_history: Anticipatory bail granted to the appellant by the High Court on 20.02.2014
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 12.03.2021; Supreme Court decision: 31 January 2024
legal_representation: Maninder Singh, Sr. Adv., Ms. Shirin Khajuria, Ms. Oshi Verma, Rajesh Batra, Ms. Sonia Kukreja, Rohit Chandra, Advs. for the Appellant; Siddhartha Dave, Sr. Adv., Santosh Krishnan, Simon Benjamin, Ms. Sonam Anand, Ms. Deepshikha Sansanwal, Ms. Mridul Singh, Devashish Bharuka, Ms. Sarvshree, Shobhit Dvivedi, Ms. Swati Mishra, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered under Sections 467, 468, 469 and 471 of the IPC; charge sheet filed under Sections 409, 467, 468, 471 and 420 IPC; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: FIR quashed; High Court: FIR quashed; Supreme Court: FIR quashed
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the FIR should not be quashed as the appellant was involved in criminal acts through misuse of the Power of Attorney (PoA), misappropriation of property, and fraudulent execution of a sale deed. The prosecution maintained that the appellant's actions constituted criminal offenses under Sections 409, 467, 468, 471, and 420 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant was merely a vendee who had no role in the execution of the PoA or any misdeed by the PoA holder. They contended that the dispute was purely civil between the land-owners and the PoA holder, and that the FIR was an abuse of the process of law. The defence also highlighted that the sale deed was valid and that the civil suit against the PoA holder had been dismissed in favor of the appellant.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that criminal prosecution should not be used to resolve civil disputes, and that the findings of a civil court should be considered relevant in criminal proceedings, provided they meet the conditions of Sections 40 to 43 of the Evidence Act. The Court also emphasized that the earlier clauses of a deed prevail over later clauses if they cannot be reconciled.
precedent_relied_upon: Mukul Agrawal v State of Uttar Pradesh, (2020) 3 SCC 402; K G Premshankar v Inspector of Police, [2002] 2 Suppl. SCR 350 : (2002) 8 SCC 87; Smt. Raj Kumari Vijh v Dev Raj Vijh, [1977] 2 SCR 997 : (1977) 2 SCC 190; Radha Sundar Dutta v Mohd. Jahadur Rahim, [1959] 1 SCR 1309 : AIR 1959 SC 24; Forbes v Git, [1922] 1 AC 256
